opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so when we started Chai, we knew the long-term goal was a lot bigger than any single model. We wanted to get to the point where we could actually design molecules, antibodies and so on, and that requires a really serious stack underneath. You need data pipelines, training infrastructure that scales, evaluation harnesses you trust, and ways to serve models to people who will actually use them.

The first model, Chai-1, was a structure prediction model in the AlphaFold 3 lineage. Part of the reason we picked that as our first project was that it's a well-defined problem. There are established benchmarks, people know what good looks like, and you can tell pretty quickly whether you're on track. That gave us a clean target to build everything around.

So in a sense, the model was the forcing function. To train something at that level, we had to build the data processing for the PDB and multiple sequence alignments, figure out distributed training, set up careful evals so we weren't fooling ourselves with leakage, and build an inference path that could handle real inputs, including things like restraints and different molecule types. Every one of those pieces is something we reuse now.

And honestly, it was also a way to learn as a team. You learn a lot about how people work together, where the bottlenecks are, what breaks at scale, when you have a concrete deliverable with a deadline. If we'd jumped straight to the much harder design problem, we'd have been debugging infrastructure and science at the same time without a clear signal of what was wrong.

Then open-sourcing it was a nice bonus. We got a lot of feedback from the community, people stress-testing it in ways we hadn't thought of, and that fed right back into making the platform more robust for everything we've built since.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls the first model “the forcing function” and explains that building it required Chai to develop reusable data, training, evaluation, and inference infrastructure.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when we started Chai, we actually made a conscious decision not to spend the first six months doing pure research. We knew the architecture space for structure prediction pretty well, and honestly the hard part wasn't going to be inventing a new attention mechanism. The hard part was going to be the plumbing.

So we treated Chai-1 as a forcing function. If you commit to shipping a model that people outside the company are going to run on real drug discovery problems, you can't hand-wave the data pipeline anymore. You have to actually figure out how you're pulling from the PDB, how you're handling the MSA generation at scale, how you're doing templates, how you're going to cluster and deduplicate and hold out a clean test set. All of that stuff that in an academic setting you'd kind of do once in a notebook and never touch again, we had to build so it would run reproducibly, every week, as the data grew.

And the same thing on the training side. Getting a model like this to train stably across a lot of GPUs, with the diffusion head and the trunk and all the different losses, that exposed every weakness in our infra immediately. Checkpointing, logging, evaluation harnesses that actually tell you something meaningful rather than just a loss curve. We built all of that against a concrete target instead of in the abstract, which I think is the only way it actually gets built well.

The other piece was inference. We open-sourced the model, which meant people were going to run it in environments we didn't control. That forced us to think about what a clean serving path looks like, what the inputs really need to be, how you expose things like constraints or restraints in a way that a medicinal chemist can actually use. That work carried over directly into the product.

So by the time Chai-1 was out, the model itself was almost the least important artifact. What we really had was a pipeline from raw structural data all the way to a served prediction, and every subsequent model we've trained has basically been a change to one or two components of that pipeline rather than starting over. That compounding is the whole point. The first model is expensive, the second one is a lot cheaper, and the tenth one is where you actually start moving fast.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls Chai-1 a “forcing function” and describes building the data, training, evaluation, and serving pipelines needed to ship it.

astra-6.text:
We saw the first model as a way to exercise the whole stack. You can build infrastructure in isolation, but until you’re trying to train a model and get it into people’s hands, you don’t really know where the gaps are. Having that concrete target forced us to work through the data pipeline, training, evaluation, and serving together.

So the value wasn’t just the model itself. It was also having a working path from a research idea to something we could actually deploy. Then, for the next model, we could build on that foundation instead of rebuilding the infrastructure every time.

r001.rationale: It says the first model was a concrete target that forced the team to exercise and develop the full stack, including training, evaluation, and serving, as a path to deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
We saw the first model as a way to exercise the whole system end to end. You can design infrastructure in the abstract, but until you’re training something real, you don’t really know where the gaps are. You have to get the data pipeline working, run experiments, recover from failures, evaluate checkpoints, and ultimately serve the model.

So the model was both a scientific project and a forcing function for building the company’s production infrastructure. The goal was to come out of that process with a model we could use, but also with a foundation that would make the next model much easier to build.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls the first model a “forcing function” for building Chai’s production infrastructure.
